title: String
html:
String problems are about finding a pattern inside a text without re-comparing characters you have already looked at. Naive matching restarts from scratch after every mismatch; Rabin–Karp compares hashes first; KMP precomputes exactly how far the pattern can safely slide. Around them sit the classic sliding-window and counting problems: anagram search, longest distinct substring and the lexicographic rank of a string.

Pattern searching — given a text txt of length n and a pattern pat of length m (1 ≤ m ≤ n), report every index i such that txt[i..i+m−1] == pat. There are n − m + 1 candidate positions.

The landscape of pattern-searching algorithms

PreprocessingAlgorithmTimeNotes
nonenaiveO((n − m + 1) · m)simple; the bound is tight for txt = aaaa…, pat = aaab
nonenaive, pattern characters distinctO(n)after a mismatch at j, slide by j
patternRabin–KarpO((n − m + 1) · m) worst, O(n + m) expectedcompares a rolling hash first; great for many patterns of the same length
patternKMP (Knuth–Morris–Pratt)O(n + m) guaranteedLPS array tells how far to fall back; never re-reads a text character
textsuffix tree / suffix arrayO(m) per query after O(n) buildwhen the same text is searched for many patterns
Key point

Preprocess whichever side is reused. One text, many patterns → preprocess the text (suffix structures). One pattern, many texts (or a streaming text) → preprocess the pattern (KMP, Rabin–Karp).

Naive pattern searching

Example

Input: txt = "GEEKSFORGEEKS", pat = "EKS"
Output: 2 10
Input: txt = "AAAA", pat = "AAA"
Output: 0 1
Input: txt = "geeks for geeks", pat = "geeks"
Output: 0 10

Library search already does this: Python's str.find(pat, start) repeated from pos + 1 finds every (possibly overlapping) occurrence.

Idea

Try every start i from 0 to n − m. Compare pat[0..m−1] with txt[i..i+m−1] character by character and stop at the first mismatch. Report i when all m characters matched. (The original notes printed inside the inner loop, which reports a hit only when the last compared character happens to be the final one — the report belongs after the inner loop.)

Time O((n − m + 1) · m)Space O(1)
Key point

The worst case needs a text and pattern that agree for a long time before each mismatch — txt = "AAAAAAAAAB", pat = "AAAB" compares m characters at almost every start. On typical text the first character already mismatches and the naive search runs close to O(n).

Improved naive when the pattern's characters are distinct

Example

Input: txt = "ABCABCDABCD", pat = "ABCD"
Output: 3 7
Input: txt = "AAAB", pat = "AB"
Output: 2

Idea

Suppose the comparison at start i fails at position j > 0, so txt[i..i+j−1] == pat[0..j−1]. Could a match begin at i + s for some 1 ≤ s < j? It would need txt[i+s] == pat[0], but txt[i+s] = pat[s], and all pattern characters are distinct, so pat[s] ≠ pat[0]. Therefore the next possible start is i + j: slide by j instead of 1. Every text character is now compared at most twice, giving O(n).

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

The original notes ran this with pat = "geeks" — whose e repeats — so the precondition was violated (and the Python for j in range(m) loop could never reach j == m). With a repeated character, sliding by j can skip a real match: txt = "aab", pat = "ab" fails at j = 1 on start 0 and would jump to start 1 — fine here, but txt = "aaab", pat = "aab" fails at j = 2 and skips the match at 1. That is exactly the gap KMP closes.

Rabin–Karp with a rolling hash

Example

Input: txt = "geeks for geeks", pat = "geeks"
Output: 0 10
Input: txt = "GEEKSFORGEEKS", pat = "EKS"
Output: 2 10
Input: txt = "aaaaab", pat = "aaaa"
Output: 0 1

Like the naive algorithm, slide the pattern over every start — but compare a hash of the pattern with a hash of the current window first, and only compare characters when the hashes agree. The trick is computing the next window's hash from the previous one in O(1) — a rolling hash.

1
A first attempt: the sum of character codes
t(i+1) = t(i) + txt[i+m] − txt[i] — O(1) per shift, but every anagram of the pattern (abc, bca, cab) has the same hash, so spurious hits are common.
2
A better hash: treat the window as a base-d number
h(s) = s[0]·d^(m−1) + s[1]·d^(m−2) + … + s[m−1]·d^0. With d = 5 and a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, d = 4: h("abc") = 1·25 + 2·5 + 3 = 38, h("dab") = 4·25 + 1·5 + 2 = 107. Position now matters.
3
Roll it
Remove the leading digit, shift left, append the new digit: t(i+1) = d · (t(i) − txt[i] · d^(m−1)) + txt[i+m]. Three multiplications and two additions — O(1) whatever m is.
4
Keep numbers small
Take everything modulo a prime q (d = 256 for bytes, q = 101 in the examples). Equal hashes are then only probably equal strings — the character check settles it.
t(i+1) = ( d · ( t(i) − txt[i] · d^(m−1) ) + txt[i+m] ) mod q
Idea

Hashing shifts the cost from O(m) per window to O(1) per window plus O(m) only when the hashes collide. A good hash collides rarely, so the expected time is O(n + m); with a bad hash (or an adversarial input) every window collides and it degrades to the naive O(n · m). The program below also reports spurious hits — windows whose hash matched but whose text did not.

Time O(n + m) expected, O(n · m) worstSpace O(1)
Key point

Window 5 of GEEKSFORGEEKS is SFO, which happens to hash to the same value as EKS modulo 101 — a spurious hit caught by the character comparison. A larger prime (10^9 + 7 with 64-bit arithmetic) makes such collisions rare in practice; in C++/Java use long so d · t cannot overflow.

Pitfall

The subtraction in the rolling step makes the remainder negative in C++, Java and JavaScript (-7 % 101 == -7). Always add q back (or write ((x % q) + q) % q). Python's % already returns a non-negative result, which is why the bug does not show in Python prototypes.

KMP: the LPS array (longest proper prefix which is also a suffix)

Example

Input: pat = "ababc"
Output: lps = [0, 0, 1, 2, 0]
Input: pat = "aaaa"
Output: lps = [0, 1, 2, 3]
Input: pat = "abacabad"
Output: lps = [0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0]

A proper prefix of a string is a prefix that is not the whole string; likewise for suffixes. For "abc": proper prefixes "", "a", "ab"; proper suffixes "", "c", "bc". lps[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of pat[0..i] that is also a suffix of pat[0..i].

Computing each entry by brute force — try every length from i down to 1 and compare — is simple but cubic:

Time O(n³)Space O(n)
Idea

Build lps left to right, reusing the previous answer. Let len = lps[i−1] — the prefix pat[0..len−1] matches the suffix ending at i−1. If pat[len] == pat[i], that match extends by one: lps[i] = len + 1. Otherwise fall back to the next shorter candidate: the longest proper prefix-suffix of pat[0..len−1], which is lps[len−1], and compare again. Fall back until a match or len == 0.

Time O(m)Space O(m)
Key point

Why O(m) despite the inner fall-back loop: len increases at most once per character (by 1) and every fall-back strictly decreases it, so the total number of fall-backs over the whole run is at most m. The same argument gives the linear bound for the matching phase below.

KMP string matching

Example

Input: txt = "abcdefg", pat = "bcd"
Output: 1
Input: txt = "aaaaab", pat = "aaaa"
Output: 0 1
Input: txt = "aaaaabaaaaac", pat = "aaaa"
Output: 0 1 6 7

Idea

Run two indices, i over the text and j over the pattern. On a match advance both. On a mismatch with j > 0, the characters txt[i−j..i−1] equal pat[0..j−1] — and lps[j−1] says how long a prefix of the pattern is still aligned with the end of that stretch. So set j = lps[j−1] and compare again without moving i. When j reaches m report i − m and continue the same way (j = lps[m−1]) to find overlapping occurrences. i never moves backwards, so the text is read once.

Time O(n + m)Space O(m)
Pitfall

After a full match do not reset j = 0 — that misses overlapping occurrences (aaaa in aaaaab occurs at both 0 and 1). j = lps[m − 1] keeps the longest reusable overlap. And guard the mismatch branch with j != 0 before indexing lps[j − 1].

Anagram search

Example

Input: txt = "geeksforgeeks", pat = "forg"
Output: Yes (window "forg" at 5)
Input: txt = "geeksforgeeks", pat = "rseek"
Output: No

Does the text contain any permutation of the pattern as a substring? Order no longer matters, only the multiset of characters, so hashing by comparison fails and we count instead. Naive: for every window, count the pattern's characters up and the window's characters down and check that everything cancels.

Time O((n − m + 1) · (m + CHAR))Space O(CHAR)
Idea

Sliding window of size m with two count arrays: cp for the pattern (fixed) and ct for the current window. Moving the window one step changes two counts in ct (one character in, one out) — O(1). After each move compare ct with cp; a window is an anagram exactly when the two arrays are equal.

Time O(n · CHAR)Space O(CHAR)
Key point

CHAR is a constant, so this is linear — but comparing 256 counters per window is the dominant cost. The standard refinement keeps a single mismatches counter: when a count in ct changes, update whether that slot agrees with cp; the window is an anagram when mismatches == 0. That is O(n) with no array comparison at all.

Lexicographic rank of a string

Example

Input: s = "ABC"
Output: 1
Input: s = "BAC"
Output: 3
Input: s = "STRING"
Output: 598

Among all permutations of the string's characters listed in dictionary order, which position does the string itself hold (1-based)? For "ABC" the six permutations are:

RankPermutation
1ABC
2ACB
3BAC
4BCA
5CAB
6CBA

The pen-and-paper method generates every permutation and counts — O(n · n!):

Idea

Count how many permutations come before s. Every permutation that starts with a character smaller than s[0] precedes s — there are (number of smaller characters) × (n − 1)! of them. Fix s[0] and repeat on the remainder: at position i, add (smaller unused characters to the right of i) × (n − i − 1)!. A cumulative count array count[c] = number of unused characters ≤ c answers “how many smaller” in O(1); after using s[i], decrement count[c] for every c ≥ s[i].

Time O(n · CHAR)Space O(CHAR)
Pitfall

This formula assumes distinct characters. With repeats ("AAB") the count of permutations starting with a smaller character must be divided by the factorials of the repeated characters' counts. Also n! overflows a 32-bit int from n = 13 — use 64-bit integers (as above), which last until n = 20.

Longest substring with distinct characters

Example

Input: s = "abcdabc"
Output: 4 ("abcd")
Input: s = "aaa"
Output: 1
Input: s = "geeksforgeeks"
Output: 7 ("eksforg")

Find the length of the longest substring in which no character repeats. The naive version tests every substring; the better one notices that once a substring from i contains a repeat, no longer substring from i can be distinct — so it breaks out of the inner loop.

Idea

Sliding window with a last-seen index per character. Let start be the left end of the current distinct window and let j move right. If s[j] was last seen at prev[s[j]] ≥ start, the window must begin after that occurrence: start = prev[s[j]] + 1. Taking start = max(start, prev[s[j]] + 1) handles both cases in one line; j − start + 1 is the length of the longest distinct substring ending at j. Each character is visited once.

Time O(n)Space O(CHAR)
Pitfall

Writing start = prev[ch] + 1 without the max is wrong: a repeat that lies before the current window (prev[ch] < start) must not pull start backwards. In "abba" at j = 3 the earlier a is at 0, but the window already starts at 2.

Interview Q&A

KMP or Rabin–Karp — when do you pick which?

KMP gives a guaranteed O(n + m) for one pattern and is the safe default. Rabin–Karp shines when you search for many patterns of the same length at once (hash each pattern into a set, then one rolling pass over the text), or for 2-D / plagiarism-style matching where hashes of many windows must be compared. Its worst case is O(n · m), so it is a poor fit for adversarial inputs.

What exactly does lps[i] mean, and why is it the right amount to fall back?

lps[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of pat[0..i] that is also a suffix of it. On a mismatch after matching j characters, the text we just consumed ends with pat[0..j−1]; its longest proper prefix-suffix (lps[j−1] characters) is the longest stretch of that text that could still be the beginning of a match. Anything longer is ruled out by maximality, and anything shorter would skip a possible match — so lps[j−1] is exactly the safe shift.

Why is KMP O(n + m) when it has a loop that does not advance i?

Charge each iteration to either i or j. Iterations that match advance i (at most n of them). Iterations that fall back strictly decrease j, and j only grows together with i, so there can be at most n fall-backs in total. The LPS construction is the same argument over m.

The Rabin–Karp hash matched but the strings differ — is the algorithm wrong?

No, that is a spurious hit, expected behaviour of any hash modulo q. Correctness comes from the character-by-character verification that runs only when hashes agree; the hash merely filters candidates. Pick a large prime (and 64-bit arithmetic) so spurious hits are rare, which keeps the expected time linear.

How would you return the anagram positions instead of Yes/No, and the substring instead of the length?

Anagram search: whenever ct == cp for the window starting at i − m, record i − m and continue instead of returning. Longest distinct substring: whenever j − start + 1 improves best, also remember start; the answer is s[start..start+best−1]. Both keep the same complexity.

Lexicographic rank with repeated characters?

Permutations with repeats are counted by the multinomial n! / (c1! · c2! · …). At position i, for each unused character smaller than s[i], add (n − i − 1)! / Π(count of each remaining character)! where that character's count is reduced by one. Same scan, one extra division per step; precompute factorials once.
